title: What is the Testing Pyramid? A Guide for the AI Era | Greptile
summary: Learn what the testing pyramid is, its three layers, how it compares to the testing trophy and diamond, and how Greptile and TREX adapt it for AI-written code.
body_markdown:
If you're like many modern engineering teams, you've spent the last few years adopting multiple coding agents and shipping code faster than ever.


There's just one problem now: testing and review.


Fast code is good, but fast code isn't always good code. Now, you're likely realizing that the gap between "writing code" and "merging strong PRs" is wider than you'd like. The standardization you need is now in review, not code generation.


And even with automated review tools, you might see lots of bugs still slipping through to prod. The next step is to improve your code review and testing with a stronger, more standardized testing strategy.


And for that, you might start by considering the testing pyramid. In this piece, we'll walk you through what it is, how it works, and how to use it effectively in a modern context.


## What is the testing pyramid?


**The testing pyramid is a visual analogy that helps software teams decide how to allocate resources to testing.** The general idea is that more complex tests that require more resources should be done more sparingly, while simpler, faster, and easier-to-run tests should be the bulk of your testing suite.


- **Bottom layer:** Unit testing, which is fast and easy to execute. Unit tests should be done liberally, on every line of new code.
- **Middle layer:** Integration testing. More labor- and resource-intensive, so it should be done regularly, but less than unit testing.
- **Top layer:** End-to-end testing (E2E testing) is traditionally more resource- and time-intensive, so it should be done sparingly.


The testing pyramid diagram was designed by software engineer and Scrum pioneer Mike Cohn. It was initially designed as part of the Agile framework, which is why many engineering teams still use it. Importantly, it was initially designed to show the relationship between types of *automated* testing, not just any software testing.


But, like any model, it of course has some flaws too, and we'll work through those later in this piece. First, let's understand the analogy itself, because it is a helpful one:


## Layers of the test pyramid


In general, the test pyramid has three layers of automated tests:


- **Unit tests:** at the bottom, making up the bulk of your automated testing
- **Integration tests:** in the middle, with fewer integration tests than unit tests
- **UI tests, or end-to-end testing:** at the top, done sparingly (due to costs, speed, and resources, typically)


### Unit tests


**Unit tests are short, automated tests that test an isolated function, component, or other small piece of code to ensure it works properly.** They typically test whether a specific unit of code delivers the expected output based on the input. That is:


- Does the discount calculate accurately based on the price input?
- Do invalid or unexpected inputs return the appropriate error?
- Does the form recognize a valid email address format?


The testing pyramid suggests that these should form the bulk of your automated testing. That's because they're typically fast to write and run, easy to maintain, easy to automate (comparatively), and catch bugs early. By catching bugs and errors in small, individual pieces of code, debugging becomes faster: you can see exactly what broke, and how to fix it.


But unit tests have one major drawback: they only show you how the code works on its own. And no code in a real codebase works in isolation. Unit testing can't tell you anything about how this code will interact with your codebase, existing code, APIs, integrations, or any other elements.


### Integration tests


**Integration tests, sometimes called "service tests," test the integration and interactions between different parts of your system.** Unlike isolated unit tests, the goal is to make sure that all components of your system (databases, APIs, services, components, etc.) work together smoothly. For example, they might test:


- Does the code correctly deduct inventory from the database after a checkout?
- Does the microservice return the correct data from the database when called?
- Does this REST API work as expected?


In short, unit tests test *the code itself* , while integration tests make sure that code functions properly *in connection with* other components of your system and application.


Integration tests are slower and more complex to manage, but they're necessary. Avoiding them, or not doing enough of them, usually results in high numbers of hidden boundary bugs and incompatibilities at scale. Even if things work perfectly in isolation, there are dozens of reasons why something might break once it's in the "real world," communicating with other components. Integration tests help you find and fix that before it goes to prod.


### E2E testing


**End-to-end (E2E) testing is just what it sounds like: testing a feature or function of your application end to end via the user interface (UI) with all components in place.** The goal is to test your application in a real-world environment. It ensures that everything a user would need to complete an action (interacting with the UI, backend services, frontend code, components, services, APIs, databases, etc.) works together as expected.


E2E testing might test things like:


- **When a user goes through the signup workflow,** does the form validation work? Is the data provided accurately written to the database? Is the profile created as expected with the appropriate access levels and security measures?
- **When a user adds an item to cart and checks out,** does the entire checkout workflow work as expected? Do discounts function properly? Does the database update? Does the Stripe integration work as expected? Do they get an automated confirmation email? Does the confirmation page load as expected?


Instead of looking at just one component or integration, you're looking at an entire workflow from start to finish as a user would complete it, and ensuring that everything works together on the backend.


E2E tests traditionally make up the smallest piece of the testing pyramid because they're slow and resource-intensive to run, require a lot of maintenance, and tend to be[flakier than other tests](https://www.greptile.com/content-library/flaky-tests) due to the large number of components involved.


However, E2E testing is critical for release confidence and ensuring that no major bugs will hit the end user in production. Even if things look good with unit tests and integration testing, E2E can uncover real-world bugs, production auth failures, config drift, workflow failures, and environment-specific errors that can't be found elsewhere.


## Benefits of using the testing pyramid


Implementing a testing pyramid at your organization can provide a number of benefits, including:


- **Helping prioritize the right types of testing.** One of the biggest strengths of the testing pyramid is helping teams ensure they're not over-indexing on one kind of testing. Too much of any one kind is a problem; too much of the wrong kind is problematic in other ways. Yes, you could analyze your code, application and system, and team and figure out your *own* best testing balance based on your needs, but the testing pyramid provides a good guide to start from.
- **Catching more bugs.** Comprehensive and balanced testing coverage catches more bugs before things ship. If you're only doing unit testing, for example, you're missing bugs that only show up at runtime. But if you over-index on end-to-end testing, you'll catch lots of small bugs late in the process, when they could have been easily caught and fixed much earlier.
- **A balanced approach, especially in agile frameworks.** Using the test pyramid in agile can work well; it's what it was designed for. Agile relies on rapid feedback loops, adaptability, and short sprints, all of which the testing pyramid helps support. The prioritization of many fast unit tests[shifts testing left](https://www.greptile.com/content-library/shift-left-testing) , while providing faster feedback. The balance of testing types also helps support short sprints, with lots of small, fast testing and saving larger lifts (E2E testing) for the cases where it matters most.
- **Testing efficiency and coverage.** A balance of lots of unit tests, some integration testing, and few E2E tests increases overall efficiency. It reduces resource-intensive E2E tests, while still ensuring you're covering all your bases for a secure and functional codebase. It helps avoid anti-patterns, like the "ice cream cone," where too much time is spent on manual testing and complex E2E testing for bugs and errors that could have been caught with simpler methods.
- **Optimized resource allocation.** In short, you spend the most time on the testing with the highest ROI, while performing a high volume of the easiest types of testing. That way, you get the most bang for your buck.


## Drawbacks and alternatives to the testing pyramid


In recent years, the testing pyramid has gathered more opposition, mainly for reasons like:


- **Test flakiness.** The larger your automated test suite, the flakier it's going to be overall. E2E testing is notoriously flaky (though more recent E2E solutions are helping fix this), which adds another layer to the problem. And test flakiness can make your testing suite less effective and, worse, less trustworthy over time.
- **Misalignment with modern architecture.** The test pyramid was invented when most codebases had the same structure (monoliths). Now, a heavy reliance on distributed cloud systems, APIs, and even AI means that testing needs to be distributed differently.
- **Over-emphasis on unit tests.** When testing was expensive and time-consuming, unit tests were (and still are) mostly fast and easy. It made sense to lean on them. But[many devs today agree](https://softwareautomation.notion.site/What-are-your-thoughts-on-the-Testing-Pyramid-How-do-your-thoughts-compare-to-what-you-see-in-reali-3fb0d2950e654571acf2d3ba1c413a16) that the focus has shifted to integration testing, which is now just as simple, more effective, and tests what you need without taking too long.
- And of course, the classic flaw of being **overly optimistic.** While it's a useful model, many devs agree that it falls short in reality: either due to resources, the reality of a complex and messy codebase, leadership desires, tight timelines, different needs, lack of implementation… the list goes on.


### Testing pyramid vs. testing trophy vs. testing diamond


A modern alternative to the testing pyramid is the **testing diamond** or the **testing trophy.** Both alternatives place the emphasis on automated **integration tests** , rather than on isolated unit tests.


The testing diamond emphasizes integration tests as the bulk of automated testing, with smaller elements for E2E and unit tests. In this model, both E2E and unit tests are only used for crucial, complex user flows or code, rather than on every line.


The testing trophy follows a similar pattern, and integrates **static testing** to form the "base" of the trophy.


This emphasizes a more modern approach, where[automated static testing](https://www.greptile.com/content-library/code-quality-tools) , like linters and SAST analysis, can catch common, small errors quickly. The other main focus is on integration testing, which ensures the code works and functions properly in connection with other services and application components.


A smaller portion of testing time is dedicated to unit testing and E2E testing, basically on an as-needed basis.


## Is the testing pyramid still useful for modern software development?


All that said: the testing pyramid was first popularized in 2009, when only 15% of US households owned a smartphone, Windows 7 was a brand-new OS, and JavaScript still lagged behind Java in terms of adoption. So is the testing pyramid still relevant?


As a model, the testing pyramid can be helpful. All models are fallible, but they can still be helpful as a framework, a starting point, or a benchmark.


However, the testing pyramid is also a product of its time: a time when computers were slower, testing was often slow and resource-intensive, most codebases were monoliths, containerization tools didn't exist, and cloud infrastructure was still nascent.


All of this makes certain elements of the testing pyramid obsolete. For example:


- Integration is far more important now, requiring more testing
- Many types of testing are cheaper, faster, and easier, making them more feasible to execute more frequently (i.e., E2E)
- There are far more automated testing options available
- Improved test frameworks make many types of testing (i.e., integration tests) easier to write, run, and maintain
- Codebases and applications are built in more varied ways. There's no one "standard" now, which means different teams need different testing structures and frameworks.
- Stronger code review and testing at various stages of the SDLC have shifted testing and review left overall, and made it easier to catch small failures much earlier on.
- Stronger debugging tools, artifacts, and AI have made identifying root causes easier, reducing the need for excessive unit tests.


None of this means the testing pyramid is obsolete. But it does change the way you think about implementing it. Instead of sticking to a strict 70/20/10 framework, you can use the types of tests you need for what you need to find, and use the test pyramid as a general guideline of how many of each type of test you're likely to need.


## Best practices for implementing the testing pyramid


So, how do you implement the testing pyramid in a modern engineering team? Here's our advice:


-


**Start by shifting testing left.**[Shift-left testing](https://www.greptile.com/content-library/shift-left-testing) makes it easier to implement unit testing early on. Test your code in small batches when it gets written (and is cheaper and easier to fix). Modern unit testing tools that integrate with pull request reviews and automate unit tests make this easier.


-


**Choose the right test for what you need to find out.** Never write more unit tests just to "adhere to the test pyramid." Remember, it's a model, not a requirement. If you need to test a REST API, write an integration test, not an E2E test. If you need to see how the workflow fits together, unit test the individual pieces first, then use the E2E test to catch what the unit tests can't.


-


**Use the lowest level of testing needed most of the time.** This is an old rule that stands the test of time. Most of the time, you use the lowest level of testing needed.


This holds true from automated testing in the test pyramid all the way down to basic code review like AI code reviewers and static linters. If you can use a linter to catch the error, don't leave it for your code review tool. If you can catch it with an AI code review tool like Greptile, catch it then, don't wait for manual QA testing, and so on. If you can catch bugs earlier with better review and automated testing, devs get instant feedback, you get better coverage with the fewest resources, and you can fix issues quickly.


-


**Choose the right level of testing.** Prioritize high levels of review and testing (i.e.,[Apex Greptile reviews](https://www.greptile.com/blog/introducing-plus-and-apex) + TREX for complete code review + E2E sandbox testing) for critical infrastructure, crucial user functions, and high-risk code changes. Use automated reviews and fixes and lower levels of testing on simple, low-risk PRs and features.


For example, Coinbase's team uses a security risk framework to score every change and PR and then adjust reviewer requirements accordingly. For low-risk changes, a single AI reviewer can look it over and implement changes. For high-risk code, they require multiple mandatory human reviewers \[1\].


-


**Use sandbox testing for realistic environments.** Integration and end-to-end testing require real (or realistic) environments to produce reliable results.[Sandbox testing](https://www.greptile.com/content-library/what-is-a-sandbox) makes this faster, easier, and more scalable. Even better, automated sandbox testing (i.e., using[TREX](https://www.greptile.com/trex) ) can spin up sandboxes with the necessary dependencies, services, code, and tests to execute and report on the test.


-


**Use automated runtime validation tests for faster, less resource-intensive E2E testing.** One of the biggest reasons why E2E is recommended to use sparingly is because it's slow and resource-intensive. And that's still true, compared to lightning-fast unit tests. But compared to E2E tests 20 years ago, today's tests are much faster and easier to manage. Implementing end-to-end tests with runtime validation tools like[Greptile's TREX](https://www.greptile.com/trex) or other E2E testing tools automates much of the time-consuming grunt work.


-


**Increase overall test coverage by testing every pull request.** A tool like TREX can make it easier to test more of your code, with more comprehensive testing, by testing at the PR stage. TREX looks at the PR, your repo, your test suite, and your stack to figure out what needs to run, then spins up the sandbox and tests, executes them, and comes back with receipts and screenshots of what happened. It makes testing faster and more efficient, giving you more coverage at the PR stage, and reducing your reliance on basic unit tests to cover your codebase.


-


**Automate, automate, automate.** The test pyramid has always been about automated testing. Implement modern automation and AI into your testing process whenever possible, and use it to make testing faster, and increase efficiency and coverage.


## How AI and agentic coding impact the testing pyramid


Unsurprisingly, AI and agentic coding are changing the way engineering teams use and implement the testing pyramid. But not only for the reasons you might think.


Yes, AI makes testing faster, makes it easier to implement E2E testing, and so on.


But the rise in agentic coding actually has changed the *amount* and *types* of testing most teams need.


One reason why: agentic coding requires more testing and review than human-written code. This isn't because agentic code is *bad* , but it makes mistakes humans don't, mistakes that typically get missed in a traditional code review process. It helps teams move faster, but it doesn't automatically make their codebase better, even if teams trust it to do so. For example:


- A Georgia Tech study tracked AI-introduced security vulnerabilities across tens of thousands of security advisories. In the second half of 2025, they found 18 cases; on average, roughly three per month. **By March 2026, they found 35 in a single month** \[2\].
- He et al.'s study of Cursor adoption in 806 GitHub repos found that velocity gains fade within two months of adoption. Meanwhile, **code complexity rises 41% at adoption and remains elevated** for the full observation period \[3\].
- Worse, Liu et al. tracked AI-introduced correctness and security issues across over 6,000 real production repositories from early 2025 through February 2026. Overall, out of 464,900 tracked AI-introduced issues, **22.7% still survived in the codebase in February 2026** \[4\].


**What all of this data tells us is not that AI-generated code is bad, but that it's *risky.***


What risky code requires is better review and better testing to reduce and eliminate that risk, without losing the speed and velocity that agentic code provides.


Many devs' first instinct is to move the testing pyramid 1:1 over to their agentic coding process, but that's also a mistake. One reason why: agents *love* to cheat at testing.


They write a dozen unit tests where two would do. They write the simplest possible tests. They write unit tests afterward that the code will pass, bypassing the ways the code *won't* pass it. They say the code passed the test when it didn't.


So what's the solution?


1. **Change the amount: test earlier, faster, and more.** Especially when working with agentic code, don't be afraid to put it through the wringer more than you would human-written code. Don't stall your entire CI/CD pipeline, but make the agent check its own work, then use[model inversion](https://www.greptile.com/blog/model-inversion) to have *a different* agent check it, and use multiple types of testing to ensure it integrates cleanly.
2. **Change the type: with agentic code, prioritize end-to-end testing with artifacts.** Unit tests are easy to "hack," E2E tests less so. Even better:[end-to-end testing with artifacts](https://www.greptile.com/blog/trex-code-execution) (screenshots, videos, logs, etc.) that help you validate what the agent tested, what happened, and what exactly went wrong. (Bonus: this makes identifying the issue and debugging faster, too.)
3. **Change who does it: use AI tools to make testing faster and less resource-intensive.** AI tools can help you move faster, but they can also make your testing more comprehensive and thorough. Instead of managing E2E tests manually with a traditional E2E testing tool, use AI to write, execute, and document them, and you can run them more often. This makes your testing suite less boxed-in to the pyramid shape and more fluid for your team's needs.
